title: Mallika's Questions
hookLine: a grieving father storms out on the Buddha, and a table of gamblers takes his side
carry: sorrow and joy are both born from the dear
tomorrow: the Buddha's own attendant wept at the end. was he wrong to?

cards: After a bad breakup, some people make a vow: never again, it hurts too much. Love less, hurt less. A sutta tests that plan, and it has a very odd detail.
A father's only son has died. He stops working, stops eating, and goes to the grave every day crying for his boy. The Buddha tells him that sorrow and grief are born from the ones who are dear.
The father storms out. On his way, he passes a group of gamblers and tells them what happened. And the gamblers agree with him, not with the Buddha.
Joy comes from the dear, they say, not grief.

teach.h: THE KING SIDES WITH THE GAMBLERS.
teach.b: So who's right? The story travels until it reaches the palace. King Pasenadi hears it and sides with the gamblers.
His queen, Mallika, does something clever. She doesn't argue. She asks him questions.
Would you grieve if something happened to your daughter? Yes. To me?
Then that is what the Buddha meant, she says. And the king sees it. Here's the puzzle solved.
The father and the gamblers each held half of the truth. The gamblers were right that joy comes from the ones we hold dear.
The Buddha was saying the same doors open both ways: the more dear someone is, the deeper the sorrow when they go. The sutta doesn't say stop loving.
Mallika keeps loving the king, and the king keeps loving his family.

teach.h: THE SAME DOOR OPENS BOTH WAYS.
teach.b: It just won't pretend love and loss can be pulled apart.
Turn that around and you get today's line.
Grief is the other side of love. If it hurts this much, it's because they mattered this much. The tradition's deeper hope is a love that holds without clutching.
But the first honest step is the one Mallika took: naming what the tears are made of.

how: Buddhist teachers often turn to this sutta when talking with people in grief; it is read as a plain description of how sorrow arises from what is dear, not as a rule against love.

o: a sign that you loved someone in the wrong way
a feeling you should outgrow by practicing harder
the hurt of loss is the other side of having loved

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: joy comes from the dear, not grief
sorrow is born from the dear

s: the sutta tells people to stop loving so they won't grieve
it never says stop loving. Mallika keeps loving the king; the point is that love and loss can't be pulled apart.
in the story, the gamblers sided with the grieving father
they said joy comes from the dear. half the truth, as it turns out.
Mallika won the king over by arguing with him
she asked him questions about his own family, and he saw it himself.

games.q: your cousin's dog died and he says he'll never get another pet. it hurt too much. what would Mallika's questions help him see?
o: he's right; the wise choice is to stop getting attached to anything.
the hurt is the size of the love; it doesn't mean the love was a mistake.
he should get a new dog right away so the grief goes away faster.
games.why: the sutta doesn't argue for loving less. it shows joy and sorrow come through the same door: the ones who are dear.

practice: Take a pen and something to write on. Write the name of one person or animal you've lost, or one you're afraid to lose. Under it, write one plain thing you loved about them: a laugh, a habit, the way they said your name.
Let the rest of the sit be for reading those two lines slowly.

wordCard.voice: Grief is love: the line Queen Mallika helped a king see. Sorrow is born from the ones who are dear, and so is joy.

orig.note: Pali piya: dear, beloved. the sutta's name means 'born of the dear'.

carryVoice: For today: sorrow and joy are both born from the dear. Grief isn't a flaw in the loving; it's the shape of it. Day fifteen of thirty, held.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 87, Piyajatika Sutta (the grieving father, the gamblers, King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika)
